opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it is that a scout isn't really one search; it's an ongoing job. You tell it something you care about, like "let me know when a new apartment in this neighborhood shows up under this price," or "track new papers on this topic," and it has to keep doing that reliably, day after day. That doesn't map well onto a single model call or even a single agent.

So we break it into pieces. There's an orchestrating layer that understands what the user actually wants and turns it into a plan: which sources are worth checking, how often, and what counts as "new" or "relevant." Then there are sub-agents that do the legwork: some issue searches, some navigate to pages and read them, sometimes actually operating a browser when the information isn't sitting in a search index. Each one comes back with what it found.

The part people underestimate is what happens after that. You need a step that compares the results against what the scout has already reported, so you're not spamming someone with the same thing three days in a row. You also need a verification step that asks, "Does this actually meet the criteria the user gave?" Agents are pretty good at finding candidates. They're less good at being disciplined about relevance unless you build that check in explicitly.

Splitting it this way also helps with cost and latency. Not every step needs the biggest model. Deciding whether a page changed can be cheap, and the more expensive reasoning happens only when something looks promising. When you're running these continuously for lots of users, that matters a lot.

And from a product perspective, the multi-agent structure gives us places to put the human back in. If a scout reports something and the user says "not quite," that feedback goes back to the planning layer, and the scout gets sharper over time. So it's less a fixed pipeline and more a little team that keeps working on your behalf and learns what you care about.

r001.rationale: It says results are compared against what the scout has already reported to avoid repeating them.

r002.rationale: It says agents return findings and user feedback can sharpen the planning layer, but does not state that the orchestrator revises its plan based on information returned by agents.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes searches through an index from navigating pages and using a browser when information is not in the index.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about scouts is that they're really a change-detection problem dressed up as a search problem. A user comes to us and says, "Keep an eye on this for me." Maybe it's a topic they care about, a product they're waiting on, a competitor, a question that doesn't have a clean answer yet. And the naive thing would be to just re-run a search on a schedule and dump the results on them. But that's not actually what anyone wants. What they want is to know when something meaningful has changed since the last time they looked.

So the pipeline splits into a few roles, and it turns out it's much easier to get good behavior if those roles are handled by separate agents rather than one giant prompt. There's a planning agent whose job is to take the user's intent and turn it into a set of concrete queries. People describe what they want pretty vaguely, and a single query almost never covers it, so you want something that decomposes the intent, thinks about synonyms, about different angles, about which sources tend to surface this kind of information. Then there's the execution layer, which is honestly the least interesting part, just agents going out and fetching, reading, extracting. The interesting part comes after that.

The third role is a diffing or synthesis agent. It has access to what we found last time, and it has to decide: is this new? Is it actually relevant to what the user asked, or is it just topically adjacent? And is it worth interrupting someone over? That last question is the hard one. Because the failure mode for anything recurring is noise. If you send someone three updates that aren't really updates, they stop reading the fourth one, and at that point the product is dead. So we spend a lot of effort on the judgment layer, on being willing to say "nothing happened" and have that be a perfectly good outcome.

One thing I've come to believe pretty strongly is that the handoffs between agents are where you get most of your leverage. Each agent sees a clean, narrow task, and that makes evaluation tractable. I can look at the planner's queries in isolation and ask whether they're good. I can look at the synthesis step and ask whether it correctly identified what was new. If it were one end-to-end model call, I'd have a lot of trouble figuring out which part went wrong when the output is bad.

There's also a memory piece that's easy to underestimate. A scout that runs for weeks accumulates context, both about the topic and about the user, like what they ignored, what they reacted to. Feeding that back into the planner so the queries get sharper over time is, I think, where these things go from being a nice feature to actually feeling like an assistant who's been paying attention.

r001.rationale: The response says synthesis uses what was found last time and that memory about user reactions can sharpen future queries, but it does not state that prior reports to the user are used as context.

r002.rationale: It describes planning queries and using accumulated context to sharpen them over time, but does not say the orchestrator revises its plan based on information returned by agents.

r003.rationale: Agents are described as fetching, reading, and extracting, but the response does not specify that they interact with the live web or distinguish that from searching a prebuilt index.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it as a coordination problem. You have a recurring task—look for new information—and you can break that into smaller responsibilities. One agent might identify what to search for, others might explore different directions, and another might bring the results together.

The interesting part is what happens across runs. What have we already seen? What has changed? Is that change useful enough to bring to the user’s attention? You need some shared memory, otherwise you’re repeatedly discovering the same things.

And I wouldn’t assume that more agents necessarily make this better. The decomposition has to earn its complexity. Parallel searches can help with coverage, but you also need a way to resolve overlap, check the evidence, and produce something coherent. Ultimately, the measure is whether the user gets useful new information with less effort.

r001.rationale: The response says shared memory is needed to avoid repeated discoveries, but does not state that prior reports to the user serve as context for later searches.

r002.rationale: It describes agents dividing search tasks and combining results, but does not say the orchestrator revises its plan based on information returned by agents.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish searching the live web from searching a prebuilt web index.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t have enough context about scouts to describe their specific workflow. But I’d think about recurring web searches as a coordination problem: what should each agent look for, what information should they share, and how do you bring their findings together? You also need some memory of what’s already been found, so the next search can focus on what’s changed. The interesting question is where multiple agents actually help—whether they bring different perspectives or cover different parts of the search—and where they just duplicate effort.

r001.rationale: It mentions keeping memory of what has already been found, but does not say the searches use the history of what scouts reported to the user as context.

r002.rationale: It discusses sharing and combining findings and focusing later searches on changes, but does not state that an orchestrator revises its plan based on information returned by agents.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish direct interaction with the live web from searching through a prebuilt web index.
